lesson.title: Rhetorical Structure: Building to a Climax
lesson.subject: ela

contentBlocks.text: Last week you built research skills. This week: advanced rhetorical analysis, going beyond Grade 9's ethos-pathos-logos basics!

Beyond WHAT appeals a speaker uses (ethos, pathos, logos, from Grade 9), skilled rhetoric also depends on rhetorical structure: the ORDER ideas are presented in. A common effective structure builds toward a climax, saving the strongest, most emotionally resonant point for last, rather than opening with it. Read these two orderings of the same three points about a community garden proposal: Ordering A (cost savings, community bonding, feeding hungry families) vs. Ordering B (feeding hungry families, cost savings, community bonding). Explain which ordering builds more effectively toward a climax, and why.
You just analyzed rhetorical structure for the first time! Tomorrow we'll learn how speakers adapt their rhetoric to a specific audience.

objectives: Understand rhetorical structure as the strategic ordering of ideas, distinct from WHAT appeals are used
Identify which ordering builds more effectively toward an emotional climax, with reasoning
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review Grade 9's ethos-pathos-logos content briefly.
2. Introduce rhetorical structure and the build-to-a-climax pattern.
3. Have the child compare the two orderings and explain which builds better.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's audience-adaptation lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: ask the child which of the three points (cost savings, bonding, feeding hungry families) feels most emotionally powerful on its own, before asking about ordering
Ready for more: ask the child to think of a different, original three-point argument and decide which point they would save for last, and why
Opens this week's advanced-rhetorical-analysis thread, deliberately going beyond Grade 9's WHAT-appeals-are-used content into HOW ideas are arranged
teacherGuide.answerKey: Ordering B builds more effectively toward a climax, since it saves 'feeding hungry families' — the most emotionally resonant point — for last, letting the argument end on its strongest, most memorable note, rather than opening with it and having the rest of the speech feel like a letdown by comparison.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Grade 11-12 RI.11-12.6: analyzing how style and content contribute to the power/persuasiveness of a text, opening this week's advanced-rhetorical-analysis thread.
